utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecution against Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to welcome all those present, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused. We're going to hear a witness today and start off with that. The Trial Chamber has found several kilogrammes of documents on its table which we're going to examine in due course. As I've already said, I said yesterday, we rendered a decision with respect to the duration of the trial, and in conformity with that, there will be 190 hours for the Prosecution to present its evidence, and we're going to try and speed up the proceedings and use some of the technical measures, and we're going to bring in one or two viva voce witnesses. That will be a technical measure. Then we will round it off with 92 ter witnesses and the 92 bis witnesses. So that is food for thought for the Prosecution, because I'm sure that is an interesting route to explore. And we're going to look at all the objections made with respect to the cross-examination, et cetera. Now, as far as the exhibits are concerned, the ones that you wish to tender will be on a list, on a document, and the registrar will give an IC number, which he has done, and the registrar can go through them document by document and give us IC numbers for them with respect to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The parties have provided the registry with lists of documents to be tendered through Mr. Safet Idrizovic. The documents provided by 1D will be given IC 78; the documents provided by 2D will be given IC 79; documents provided by 3D will be IC 80; the documents by 4D, IC 81; documents by 5D, IC 82; documents by 6D, IC 83. 3D has also provided a list for documents to be tendered through Mr. Fahrudin Agic; that will be given IC 84. The Office of the Prosecutor has provided a list of documents to be tendered through Witness BZ, and that will be IC 85. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Mundis, the witness that will be shown in will receive the same protective measures? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My colleague Mr. Poryvaev will be taking the witness. The witness -- perhaps it's best for my colleague to explain it. But with respect to the documents, the Prosecution proposes that the documents can be discussed in open court. We would ask that they not be broadcast outside the courtroom and that they be placed under seal, pursuant to the request of the Rule 70 provider. This would be very similar to the method that was used with an earlier Rule 70 witness. With respect to any other protective measures, my colleague Mr. Poryvaev will be in a position to address those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But I think we should go into private session for some moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you were overtaking your functions from your predecessor, did you overtake all the documentation that was at the disposal of your predecessors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. As I said, during the -- when we were still in Spain, we were receiving every single report that was produced in the area. And when we took over from the previous battalion of Spain positioned there, the relief team received the entire file of documents that had been produced during that previous mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what were the main functions of your section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mission of my section was to offer the head of the battalion the information required so that he could take his decisions in an informed manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you authorised to make your own decisions when your chief, your immediate superior, was away from the area of your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Within the sphere of work carried out by my section, when the chief was away, I would assume his responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a task of interviewing local military personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I personally took part in some interviews and contacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you clarify, please, for the Trial Chamber, at what level did you have contacts with the military personnel in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took part as a member of my section in all the high-level meetings that were held involving the Spanish contingent, and I also spearheaded some medium-level meetings with local commandment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "high-level meetings," what kind of highness do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally, high-level meetings would mean those meetings where the participants were high-level politicians, holding presidential positions, such as President Izetbegovic or President Boban, or with other key commanders of the military forces, such as Halilovic and Petkovic from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who represented Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What party was represented by Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Halilovic was the commander-in-chief of the Belgrade forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the subject matter of your interviews with the local military authorities? I mean, the main subject matter or main subject matters of your talks with them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly, our mission was to facilitate or guarantee humanitarian aid flow. All of the interviews were attempting to reach agreements to enable this humanitarian aid flow to continue. This was the main objective. Obviously, to achieve this, we tried to ensure that the conflicting parties reached agreements by ceasing hostilities, and we hoped in that way that humanitarian aid would be able to circulate freely throughout the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CB, please remind the Trial Chamber what was of responsibility of SpaBat battalion, SpaBat UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our area of responsibilities for the SpaBat began in the south with the border with the Republic of Croatia, around Metkovic, and extended up to -- practically up to Sarajevo, to the south of Sarajevo in Tarcin. So our mission was to guarantee that the route following the Neretva River, which was basically from Metkovic to the suburbs of Sarajevo, remained open for the free flow of humanitarian aid convoys. Later, as the conflict progressed, at a certain point in time, we received a supplementary order which extended our responsibilities to include acting through the presence of our troops as a mitigating force for conflicts in the area, to calm the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, let's stop, because we'll continue this issue a little bit later on, I mean your additional functions. Witness, as your mission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, excuse me. Before we move to another subject, I have one question for the witness. Witness CB, you have said that you participated in high-level meetings, that is, with President Izetbegovic and President Boban, in areas where the Spanish battalion was present, and at the intermediate level with military representatives, such as Generals Halilovic and Petkovic. I just want a clarification. Did you personally take part in meetings with those personalities, or is it your section that was represented at those meetings? Maybe another person, not you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally took part in these meetings, but I should also indicate that my role in these meetings was a secondary role. The representation both of my section and of the Spanish Battalion was held by staff who had been there longer than myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness CB, as your mission was coming to the end, did you participate in the drafting of any final document as a report of the whole mission of SpaBat in the area of your responsibility as from April, 1993, through October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I took part actively and in a fundamental way in drafting the overall report concerning the work of my section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this document drafted in Bosnia-Herzegovina or already in Madrid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The drafting was completed in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to be shown Exhibit 4698A. I mean the final report of Witness CB. Just, Your Honour, for explanation, this exhibit is a full version of our previous document, Exhibit 4698, but a full version with documents added to our initial version after we requested additional documents, missing documents, on your decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please turn in this document, exhibit, to page 7. Page numbers were assigned in all versions. Witness, I don't ask you to read the names on this page, but you see here the list of staff members of your section. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, if you scroll the document down, you will see the range of information that your section was supposed to receive on a regular basis. You see here weekly "Infsum, daily information summary, daily sitrep, disposition on warring factions, current situation map, picinfsum, picinfsum Sarajevo, daily intrep." Further, you see that each information is processed and distributed to subordinate units. Is that correct? Was this information also distributed to the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These are documents that we received from the area of operations, and we distributed them to our subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like you to turn to pages 64, 66, of this same document, the same exhibit. Here, you see the sources of information that were used by your section for producing your reports. Among others, I mean various kinds of reports of deep reconnaissance unit, you see radio programmes, local press, humanitarian agencies, meetings with other platoons, exchange information with British and Canadian battalions, interviews that you have just mentioned, and information -- exchange information with ECMM, and also meetings with other sections. Are those actually the sources of your information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. Those were the sources of information that we used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Including media -- media, local media, and radio programmes, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We had interpreters whose job it was to give us a daily summary of the local media - written media, radio, and television, where available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my next question: Did you receive information from the local population by conducting -- just having contacts with them, talks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On several occasions I had the chance to meet with the local population. Over and above this, it was a standard rule in the work of the whole of the Spanish Battalion that every contact we had with the local population had to be reflected in the report, which ended up in my section, and the majority of these reports ended up being included in the final report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest that you had contacts both with the Croats and the Muslims and the Serbs in that area of your responsibility. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that all kind of information was reflected in the reports. What kind of reports were produced by your section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My section drafted mainly daily reports showing information. The information included in these reports was all information relating -- excuse me, which we considered could have had an influence in our own operations and in the distribution of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now a very important question about the grades of credibility of your reports, because you were the only section which drafted reports with certain grades of credibility. Just give the Trial Chamber a very brief overview of the grades of credibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The standard procedure in the Spanish Army is to assign to every item of information a letter and a number. The letter refers to the level of credibility of the source of the information. It goes from A to F, with the greater credibility at the top and the lower credibility at F. The number is related to the reliability of the information, of the information contained in that report. It goes from number 1, most reliable, to 6, which is the least reliable. When reports are written, while the report is being drafted, every item of -- every element included in the report is categorised in this way. When the report is completed, we look for the lowest qualification, the lowest degree, and that is applied to the overall report as a whole. That is why you can see reports which have a certain grade, but within that grade there are certain elements which might have a higher degree of reliability, but the overall grade given to the report is usually -- sorry, is always that of the level assigned to the element with the lowest grade within the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CB, I've seen a lot of reports produced by your section and noticed that most of them were given a C2 grade of credibility. That means "fairly reliable and probably true." Does it mean that, for example, you did not include information which was under F, for example, "reliability cannot be judged," or under 6, "truth cannot be judged"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's an extremely [previous translation continues], and perhaps instead of the Prosecutor putting words into the witness's mouth about whether C2 means "fairly reliable and probably true," it might be better to have the witness's own explanation of that coding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Maybe it's correct, but I think that such kind of military menus are very well known to everybody in this courtroom and no need to lose our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm afraid that's just not right, Your Honour. I'm speaking as one person to whom these things are not familiar and I associate myself with Mr. Murphy's intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay, but what is done can't be undone. The question is answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the purpose of my objection was not to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we lose time on irrelevant objections, this subject has already been dwelled upon at length. We have seen these letters and numbers many times, so maybe it makes no sense for the Prosecution to raise that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, just briefly, again, could you describe the steps of drafting your daily intreps? As an example, let's take Exhibit 0213 -- sorry, 02143. This is intrep 1, 5, and 7, the 29th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. To draft this report, we received all the reports produced by subordinate units, by patrols who, at the time, we had deployed throughout the territory in the area under our responsibility, and by individual activities that some member of the battalion had taken part in. It might be a meeting, for example. And all of these reports came to my section. From all of these reports, we extracted the information that we considered worthwhile for our commander, and using that, we drafted the report. As we selected the information to be included in our report, we graded it as we went. As I have explained, we used a letter and a number. Once we finalised the report, it was re-read and we graded it at the lowest possible ranking, and that final grade referred to the entirety of the document. As to the issue of whether there are reports with -- the fact that we don't have any reports with a lower figure, I can say that if we felt they were absolutely outrageous, we quite simply did not include them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question, Witness, is: You see an end time of 21.30. What do you mean by the "end time"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the time at which the report arrived, the last interim report arrived, which was used in creating this final summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 -- or paragraph 1, sorry, with several subparagraphs, you see, "Zone of Influence." Could you explain, what did you mean by "Zone of Influence." We know zone of responsibility or area of responsibility. Is there any difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Usually a zone of influence is broader than zone of responsibilities. Zone of influence is an area in which there are events, and these events might affect our force's activities or might lead to other happenings within our area of responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mean, for example, that you also, for example, mentioned Maglaj, Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, which were not within the area of your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, because all of the events occurring outside of our area of responsibility could, in some way or another, influence the development of events in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also you have here "Comments." What is the status of "Comments"? For example, here you have, at point such-and-such: "The HVO prevented the Spanish from continuing its march in the direction of Sovici." I'm not asking about the gist of this comment but the status of the comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What are written as news are either facts that we have observed or declarations by third parties. What is written as comments is our valuation or the valuation given by our section to those facts. This is to guide the chief concerning the significance of this information, what this information might mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then your second step, you would send this report to Kiseljak UNPROFOR headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any feedback from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Every day -- every night we completed the report and we sent it to the general barracks of UNPROFOR in Kiseljak, and the following morning, we would receive from Kiseljak the report drafted by them which covered all of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's, for example, take Exhibit 02269. This is a fax from Kiseljak, dated the 10th of May, 1993. On page 1 -- have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 1 you see that SpaBat is one of the recipients of this document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, that is correct. This is received from the UNPROFOR general barracks, and we, the Spanish Battalion, were one of the recipients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you familiarise yourself with these kinds of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my time in Bosnia, this kind of document, I read it every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this particular document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This, in form, relates to a day in May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2 of the document - again, I will not discuss the gist of the report about Mostar; I will only ask you about the source of this information - was this information provided to Kiseljak headquarters by your section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. All of this information was contained in the daily report that we sent to Kiseljak the day before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, very briefly, about the procedural drafting of insums. What is the difference between intreps and insums? As an example, let's take Exhibit 2185.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may I intervene for one second. Your Honours, as you well know, we're trying to save time. We've had a gentleman from SpaBat come over here and testify as to all these procedures. I think one question could have been asked early on, such as, "The procedure used in SpaBat, was that universal?" If the answer is yes, then obviously we can move on; otherwise, we're just repeating. I'm just trying to save some time, and I think that's the way the procedure should be from now on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas, for this observation. It follows common sense. Some of these questions have already been dealt with, so please try to follow the comment of Mr. Karnavas and focus on the main things, on the principal things, because everybody knows how things worked in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I will follow your request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only question to this document: It was drafted in Madrid. Did you receive these kinds of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As can be seen on the first page, the recipients of these documents, the first one is Jacan, the first recipient, and this is the head of the Canary Islands group, which was part of the UNPROFOR Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move on. Witness, as it's known from your witness statement, at some point you were moved to the Jablanica area. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is also well known from your statement that at some point you were wounded and then you took a leave. Did you continue receiving information about your area of responsibility afterwards? And were you updated on the events that happened in your absence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. During the time that I was in Jablanica, my second took on the responsibilities as deputy in the Medjugorje barracks, but Jablanica, that detachment received all the information produced in the Medjugorje headquarters. So I was perfectly updated about all the events occurring in that area through the reports that I received from Kiseljak, and I was informed, through the reports from my section and through Kiseljak, of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For about 30 days I was out of action, and during that time, 15 of the days I spent in the Republic of Croatia. When I was there, I did receive daily information concerning developments of events. And in the second 15 days, I was in Spain. When I was in Spain, I no longer received daily reports, but once I was reincorporated into my previous position, I received the entire file for the section. All of the elements of that section offered me a series of briefings and lectures to bring me up to date on the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Now let's move to your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I will not repeat each time Exhibit 468 -- 98A, but I will say "final report."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the importance of Jablanica in terms of its situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The city of Jablanica was a centre of communication, a very important one. It is situated on the main road linking the coast to Sarajevo and the central part of Bosnia. Furthermore, it was the headquarters of a hydro-electric station, which had a lot of strategic importance in the area. I could add that the interethnic situation in the area was very complicated, with various different communities, where you had one minority ethnicity faced with a different ethnic group. So the situation was very complicated, and this caused us not only problems but also a lot of work to be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please open your final report, on page 40. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the area of responsibility, I mean Jablanica, reflected correctly in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It accurately reflects the situation in that place at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that you just took over your functions on the 20th of April, 1993? And as from that moment, you were acting in your position; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 20th of April, 1993, is when the transfer of authority occurred. The Malaga and Canarias detachments changed over. They handed over to the Spanish Battalion that I belonged to. This transfer of authority meant that from that time onwards the Canarias detachment, which was in charge of all of the missions, the documents, et cetera, but I have to also say that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there's a problem with the sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- area of -- personnel from other sections started to contribute to the drafting of these documents. And with this transfer of authority, elements of the previous battalion remained in the section and they helped us to understand the material that we received, the information that we received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the first information received by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we appeared in the area of operations, the previous battalion informed us via briefings of their missions and operations that they were in charge of and that the Spanish Battalion was in charge of, and this included -- this included our missions and the effects on the local population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was happening in Jablanica at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time in the area of Jablanica, our colleagues informed us that they had reports of strong combatant activity from the HVO and the armija from the -- receiving orders from Sarajevo and from Slatina. They told us also that all of this information was provided by staff from outside of the SpaBat because the conflicting parties did not let the UNPROFOR troops and personnel enter into this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to open Exhibit 2008. This is intrep 148, the 21st of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3, according to -- I will help you find it. "According to Muslim sources ..." Did you receive such kinds of information from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Our colleagues in the Jablanica detachment gave us this information after having held meetings with various people in charge of armija in that town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's move to Exhibit 2012. This is intrep 149, dated the 21st of April; page 5 in the English version and page 4 in the Spanish version, the part relevant to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, "According to intelligence received from HVO ..." and further goes a description of the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the one hand we have the information regarding bombing. This is information that the Spanish personnel reports as a result of direct observation. And then in the paragraph that has other information, the information that refers to detention by the police of 15 people is also a direct observation. The remark you have there is our evaluation of this information, what it might mean. And then with the title which says "According to information received from HVO sources ..." it refers to a meeting with several members of this Croatian Defence Council, during which this information was handed to us. At the end, there is a remark which is the evaluation; in other words, what we think all this information might mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what were your personal observations at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal observations? May I stress that this is a report prepared on the 22nd of April, and at that date I was in the Medjugorje headquarters. As for the situation in Jablanica, most of the information was obtained through direct observation and contacts, that the information coming from HVO providers are contacts that existed already in the previous grouping, which, during the previous six months, these contacts had given information on a, more or less, regular basis, which was then checked and so on. Therefore, the level of credibility of this information was high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first appear in the Jablanica area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the question that the Judges have to deal with and decide about Jablanica is to know who launched the offensive. Was it the HVO or was it the BH army? On the basis of your own observations and the documents you had in your hands, who launched the offensive? That's a very clear question. Who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As far as I know, when we arrived in that area, in April, 1993, the Croatian Defence Council launched an offensive in that area, coming from the west towards the east, towards Jablanica, and mainly in the valley where we have Doljani and Sovici populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we respectfully suggest that counsel's question was an absolutely suitable introduction to Your Honour's question, that logically counsel's question, as just asked when Your Honour put his question, was exactly the right question as a lead-in to Your Honour's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a Judge asks a question, there's no need for a previous introduction. So I'd like to make that point clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question was: When did you first appear in Jablanica? And what did you see in the area of Jablanica, in the villages in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Jablanica -- I went to Jablanica on various opportunities before I was assigned to that area in full term. I can't remember exactly what the date was, but I do remember that after an agreement that was signed by Generals Halilovic and Petkovic, with our support, a series of patrols were dispatched to conflict areas. I must repeat: I don't remember the exact date, but I do remember having taken part in the patrol that went to populations of Sovici and Doljani. And I went to visit the school of Doljani where we found some 60 men, older men, who were under the custody of the Croatian Defence Council. During its activities, the patrol's activities, I was able to observe that there was dead cattle. We didn't see any human remains. The majority of the houses had been destroyed, some of them quite clearly as a result of armed weapon attacks. Others were burnt down. And along our route, our way, we had to cross various check-points under the charge of the Croatian Defence Council. And I do remember, having seen how General Halilovic addressed these older men, which were -- who were detained in the Sovici school, and I do recall we had to abandon our visit in a rush, because in the Konjic area some problems had arisen and we had to proceed in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, who else participated in that, let's say, visit to the Sovici village, from the HVO side and ABiH side and from SpaBat side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Mr. Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor asked the witness a question as to when he came to Jablanica first. The witness didn't give a date but started with his narrative. I'd like to remind him that it was the 3rd of May. So his first arrival in Jablanica was on the 3rd of May, 1993, because he never answered the Prosecutor's question when he arrived. He explained what happened when he had already arrived, but that was the date. So that's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but I don't need your assistance because I want to show the witness a document relevant to the date of this visit and the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, the problem I'm having --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the floor in just a moment, but the question General Petkovic asked, I was going to ask myself. I was wondering myself, because he said that he went to Jablanica and I asked -- I wondered whether it was before or after the offensive. I wondered that myself. And then when he went on to recount what he did, I concluded that it was after a military phase, a military stage. What was lacking was the date, and General Petkovic has just told us that the visit took place exactly on the 3rd of May, 1993. What did you want to ask, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, Mr. President. The direct examination is rather difficult to follow. Why? Because we're not getting a narrative. We spent a lot of time, almost a whole session, on going over information that we already have, explaining what this term means, what that term means, how a form is filled out. What I think would be most appropriate, both for the Trial Chamber's position and for us as well, is to get a narrative from the gentleman. Who, what, where, when, why, how; for him to tell us his story. Then you have something to work with; we have something to cross-examine on. The documents can come in a lot easier that way. But we need a narrative first. Otherwise, it becomes extremely difficult for us to figure out what we need to confront.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Karnavas, that was exactly what we were getting to when General Petkovic interrupted, and perhaps it would be good if such interruptions would really be kept to an absolute minimum. It is not possible in these proceedings, and it's not correct, that whenever a witness says something which an accused thinks is not correct that he immediately intervenes and tries to rectify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I totally agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the Prosecutor needs to control the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He's directing. What happened? When?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not contradicting you at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the witness was getting a little bit ahead of himself, and good for him, but let's be directed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Let's celebrate our accord without taking the time of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please open Exhibit 1 -- 2192.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 34 in Spanish --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that, I'd like to make some clarification. Before I was sent to Jablanica in a continuous manner, for various reasons I was able to visit Jablanica on various different occasions, but I did not stay there continuously until later on. In one of those opportunities, I was meeting in the Jablanica detachment where General Petkovic and General Halilovic took part, which we referred to before. But before that date, I had already been in that area. Of course, when we came to the operation area, the Spanish Battalion, and because of our responsibility in the section, we did some reconnoitering of the whole area. That was in the first week when I took up my functions. In that first week, I already went to Jablanica at least once. What I was referring to was being in Jablanica in a permanent position, and in that situation, I seem to remember that that was towards the middle or end of June. But that does not mean that I hadn't been in Jablanica before then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, the first time you were in Jablanica was before the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Spanish, page 34; English, page 45. Exhibit 2192, dated the 3rd of May, 1993, intrep 162. Were you present at that meeting and round of talks between Mr. Halilovic, Pasalic, Petkovic, and Lasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there was any agreement reached as a result of those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember quite clearly the agreement. Each of the parties was interested in visiting certain areas where they had carried out military actions. The armija VH [as interpeted] were interested in visiting Doljani and Sovici, and the Croatian Defence Council was interested in visiting the pockets north of Jablanica, between Jablanica and Konjic. And I do recall that the Croatian Defence Council expressly wanted to see the Konjic monastery, where there were Catholic religious officials who were being detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, was there any decision with respect to the civilians arrested in the school building? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no decision taken at that time, but I do remember that later I took part in an exchange of prisoners, or several. During these exchanges, somebody gave me the information that part of the prisoners that the Croatian Defence Council was freeing came from Doljani and Sovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CB, my next question will be: At the beginning of the examination, you said that at some point your functions, I mean your SpaBat functions, were expanded. Do you remember when it happened, and why, and to what extent your functions were extended?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we should make a break because three minutes are left, and the questions I said, the witness may have some time to think them over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's take a break, but it will be half an hour. We'll reconvene at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CB, my question before the break was: What happened that, at some point, the end of April, 1993, the functions of SpaBat UNPROFOR were expanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, the functions of SpaBat and UNPROFOR, but I'm talking more specifically about the Spanish Battalion, were to guarantee humanitarian aid flows. As the situation deteriorated, given the problems between the Croatian ethnic group and the Bosnian Muslim community, in the city of Mostar, there was a meeting. If my memory serves me correctly, it was a General Pellnas who brought this about. He was the head of the United Nations forces, and he managed to get an agreement for a cessation of hostilities signed between the Croatian defence forces and the armija, which is the forces of the Sarajevo government. One of the terms of this agreement was the presence of UNPROFOR troops within the city of Mostar, with the intention being that its mere presence would calm the situation and encourage the conflicting parties to be evermore reluctant to commit violent acts. This occurred towards the end of April. From that time onwards, apart from convoy escorts for humanitarian aid and all of the tasks associated with these escort missions, the Spanish patrols were in charge of patrolling the east and west sides of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, did you participate in any meetings that were celebrated in April, 1993, with respect to the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in particular in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, the transfer of authority from the previous Spanish Battalion to the one that I was operating in happened on the 20th of April. I personally got involved on the 19th of April. I think I remember correctly that there was this meeting under the auspices and the chairmanship of the head of the UN observers, and I think this was actually prior to my arrival. However, later, there were other meetings where both parties took part, and I did take part in those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who participated in those meetings on behalf of HVO and on behalf of ABiH and international community? And if you remember the dates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I seem to remember reading a report on this meeting, drafted by General Pellnas, who chaired the meeting as a representative of the international community of the United Nations, and by the defence -- Croatian Defence Council. I think it was Halilovic, accompanied by General Lasic, who was the local officer in charge of Mostar. On the Muslim side, I think it was Colonel or General Halilovic and Pasalic, who was in charge of the area of Mostar for those forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. According to the record, General Halilovic figures twice; I think once in a Croatian hat and then in a Muslim hat. Probably you wanted to say "Petkovic" when you said "Halilovic" the first time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm sorry, sir. The first time, on the Croatian Defence Council, it was Colonel Petkovic and Colonel Lasic, and on the armija BiH, it was Colonel Halilovic and Colonel Pasalic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I would like you to take a look at Exhibit 02054.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was the report I was talking about, personally drafted by Colonel Pellnas. As I, indeed, said, it was on the 28th of April, which is the day before I arrived in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is the date the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know about the decision made by General Pellnas as a result of his numerous meetings with representatives of both parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. A copy of the agreements, apart from the report written by Pellnas, a copy of the report came to our Spanish Battalion, and from there, that's where the order was given to deploy troops in Mostar concretely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at the same exhibit, pages 6, 7. On these pages you'll see information of some events which occurred in Hotel Mostar, in Mostar city. What really happened there? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry to interrupt you, but at least when I look at this document, 2054, I do not see here numbers as far as the pages are concerned. So I'm not quite sure -- now I may have discovered something: Very, very small letters on the right-hand side, but then I -- excuse me, then I find it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Mostar hotel, there was a headquarters for the armija BiH. In accordance with the agreement's terms, this had to be abandoned by these armija BiH troops, but they said that they could not leave it because of sniper-fire coming from the west side of the city. So General Pellnas asked the Spanish Battalion for support so that they could evacuate this building with a certain measure of safety. Indeed, protected by the Spanish Battalion, they arrived at the building. They brought out the equipment and material and evacuated them to East Mostar. With this, the Croatian defence force agreed that this particular part of the agreement had been fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CB, when did you first appear in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said before, in the first days upon our arrival in the area of operations, we carried out reconnaissance activities in the area. I cannot give you the exact date, but I know that it was in the first week of my arrival. I did go through all of the area covered by the Spanish Battalion, including all of the detachments, et cetera. And a major part of that reconnaissance activity was in the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were your personal observations in Mostar at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal impressions were that I was in a city divided, in fact, not only divided by the river, and that there was -- there were more people of Croatian descent living on the west side than the other way around, and there were Muslim people living on the east. My personal observation and those of other members of the Spanish Battalion, whose reports came to my knowledge, they saw enmity between the Croatian ethnic group and the security forces and military forces against the Muslim population. They put pressure on the Muslims in various ways, which led us to believe that the intention on the part of the Croatian forces was that the Muslims abandon the west part of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're talking about pressure in some ways by the Croats on the Muslim population, could you expand a little bit more. What do you mean by that? What kind of pressure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be able to give a concrete example, in the signed agreement, there was mention of a free circulation of people, and we're talking about civilian people between both parts of the city. A bus system was set up, under the escort of the Spanish Battalion, to transport people from one side of the city to the other. And I believe one day Croatian people wanted to go to the east side of the city, and they could do so without any major problems, and the military forces in the east side of the city, armija BiH, didn't actually put up any opposition to this movement of people. But, however, when Muslim individuals tried to cross to the west side of the city, their way was blocked by the security forces of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have talks with the local population at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. I was in contact with the local community on one side and on the other, and during these conversations I could observe that the Muslim population living in the east side of the city were living in a state of fear. They told me that there were cases of forced expulsions and members of a family could be rounded up and forced to head to the east side and live in -- and they had to leave all their belongings in their houses. There was a whole series of circumstances such as, for example, the owners of the shops and businesses in the west side of the city refused to serve Muslim customers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When talking about some agreement celebrated between the parties, I would like you to take a look at Exhibit 02012. Intrep, the 21st of April, 1993. Spanish, page 3; English, page 4-5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was this agreement fulfilled in full? I mean, in part, at least, "all civilians bearing arms shall surrender them, all matters should be completed by the 23rd of April," so on and so forth, about barricades and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, indeed, this agreement wasn't fulfilled in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were there any attempts from both sides, goodwill, just to implement that agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to make it clear that I think those that signed the agreement did have the will to implement it, but once they were signed at the general level, at the level of the generals, it's not necessary -- you don't necessarily get the same will at the medium level of command in the field. If you look at the comments, you will see that it says that the tension could lead to an outbreak of violence between these two factions or in the area between the armija and the defensive forces of Croatia, the Croatian forces in Mostar. It seemed that on the part of the Croatian defence forces, there was a real will to reach agreements. The posture, the stance, of the representative of Mostar in the Croatian defence forces was more militant and did not -- and did not seem so intent on having this implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry, but a little bit -- maybe there is some confusion or an error in the transcript. You say that "... on the part of the Croatian defence forces, there was a real will to reach agreements. The posture, the stance, of the representative of Mostar in the Croatian defence forces was more militant ..." There is something inconsistent. Maybe you will rephrase your response to make it easier to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I would like to say one thing. In the first part of the witness's answer, it is clearly stated that at the level of generals there was goodwill to reach agreements, but the problem occurred on the medium level of command. And precisely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have now understood. Very well. Can you confirm the following: At the high level of command of the HVO, you felt that they wanted an agreement; however, at the level of local commands, they were not on the same wavelength.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about the months of April and May in 1993, and the impression that we had is that the chains of command were exerting their power but tended to diminish as you went down the chain of command. My personal experience I can share with you, and that is that the meetings in which I took part, where there was Colonel Petkovic, personally, I saw a will to reach an agreement and have them implemented. I cannot say the same for other meetings in which the HVO representatives were present, and they were of a lower rank than Colonel Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just add a question. You have now referred to the Croat side. Does the same apply, in your experience, your opinion, to the ABiH side? Was there the same thinning of authority: Goodwill at the top, less goodwill farther below?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned other people from the Croatian side, the lower level, were against such kinds of agreements and implementation. For example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I repeat that my personal observations and the impression that I had from this meeting, for example, that General Lasic from the Croatian defence forces, operating in Mostar, was less inclined to sign an agreement and even implement them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, finally, the decision to expand your functions was made. Do you mean some order issued on that issue? By whom that order was issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, via the signed agreement between these two parties and chaired by Colonel Pellnas, the UNPROFOR headquarters issued an order signed by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter does not have the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And having received no news of the intentions to full out -- to fulfil these orders, the Spanish Battalion got in touch with those in charge of the Spanish mission, and having received the order and the authorisation from the Spanish forces, the order was implemented under the orders of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was General Morillon before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 02011.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, perfectly. This is the message coming from the UNPROFOR headquarters in which the Spanish Battalion is informed of the new concept of operations and in which we are ordered to deploy patrols both in Mostar and in the Jablanica/Konjic area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many patrols did you deploy in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, there was one patrol in the west side and one in the east side of the river, east and west of the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive reports from them on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. The patrols drafted reports. Once there was a change in patrol, the incoming, the returning, patrol would draft a report which described occasionally all of the incidents that had taken place, which might be contact with the local community, with the conflicting parties, their observations, et cetera, et cetera. All of this data would be drafted into a report which came to the section where I was working, and one of the sources that we used for drafting our daily report was this report from the patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, so it's a fact well known that the international community failed to prevent the armed conflict in Mostar which broke out on the 9th of May, 1993. What was the first information you got about the start of the conflict on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 9th of May, yes, indeed. This is when the conflict broke out between the two parties openly. The initial reports that we received came from the patrols in the city of Mostar which immediately reported via radio a bombardment, a very heavy bombardment, over the east side of the city. Later, the patrols' reports informed us of how events had developed throughout the city. If I remember correctly, this was in the 9th of -- the 9th -- the night of the 9th of May or the very early morning of the 10th of May. I can't remember well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was happening with the population of Mostar during these clashes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The civilian population of Mostar, mainly in the area close to the boulevard and towards the east, which were the most heavily affected areas, the local civilian population took cover as best they could, but there were a lot of casualties among the civilians. They suffered as a result of this conflict. The connection between East Mostar and the north of Bosnia, going towards Jablanica, was cut, and they started to have difficulties in the east part of the city, difficulties getting supplies, basic necessities. At one point the supply of running water was cut off in the east side and so the civilian population had to go and get water from the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's stop at that. Let's still go back to the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to take a look at Exhibit 2241. This is intrep 167, the 9th of May, 1993. English, page 4; Spanish, page 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found it? There is a comment to this document, to this passage of the document. "The HVO seems determined to take absolute control of the whole city. It seems unlikely that fighting will stop until it has achieved its objectives." What allowed your section to make such kinds of conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depending on how the fighting developed in Mostar, we had different declarations via personal contacts mainly with members of the Croatian defence forces. Personally, I remember hearing a prominent member of these defence forces saying that the Muslims already had Sarajevo and that Mostar should be Croatian. Given this data, we concluded that there was an insistent interest among the Croatian Community of Bosnia-Herzegovina to make Mostar its capital, its symbolic capital, which entailed, or at least some people felt, that it was necessary to expel anyone belonging to a different ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe any facts of expulsion of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, I don't remember seeing that personally. I do remember reading reports which stated that this was going on. I remember seeing in even television video images of these expulsions, and you could see civilians grouped together and held by Croatian defence forces in a football stadium. And I received reports, checked by myself, referring to the fact that at given points in time, the police of the Croatian defence forces were painting the houses that had housed Muslim families in the west part of the city, and that these civilians had been expelled from these houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did SpaBat have an opportunity of observing all these actions from the centre of Moscow -- sorry, Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The patrols which were in the city at the time when this strong fighting broke out and when the heavy bombardment began - and on the east side there were replications and there was an overall exchange of fire - our patrols withdrew from the danger zone and took up positions for observation from which they could observe the events happening in the city. I believe that I recall that the patrol in the west side of the city withdrew to a place around about the hospital, the Croatian hospital. From the parking of that hospital, there was an observation vision; there was a good vantage point to see most of the city. And from there we could observe the bombardments as well as the way that the Croatian defence forces herded people towards the football field near the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to take a look at Exhibit 2286. This is intsum 29; page 5 on both versions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the passage beginning with the words, "On the 9th" -- "On the day of 9th of May, at 5.00 ..." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the situation in this intsum described correctly, accurately?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before the gentleman answers the question, I'm not sure that I understood whether the gentleman was in Mostar at the time. Now he's being asked to verify what's in a report of which he wasn't an observer of. I think that, you know, it's one thing for him to describe what he was told, what was put in the report, but now he's being asked to vouch for the contents in the report, and I think there is a distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I disagree with Mr. Karnavas, because before this, just some minutes ago, the witness just told the Trial Chamber that he was receiving reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try and shed some light on the matter, in order to save time. Sir, on the 9th of May, 1993, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the headquarters of the Spanish Battalion in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. At the headquarters of Spanish Battalion in Medjugorje, did you have constant contacts with units of the BritBat in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Now, how did you establish that contact, by radio or how else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By radio, Your Honour. Apart from the patrols that when they returned, they gave reports immediately. So we had occasional information by radio and we had more detailed information in written reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the basis of what you've just told us, the Judges of this Trial Chamber, can they draw the conclusion that at the headquarters of the Spanish Battalion, they were specifically informed about the developments on the ground, whether they be combats or general events on the ground? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Spanish Battalion -- sorry, the headquarters of the Spanish Battalion were perfectly and occasionally informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer my question as for Exhibit 2286, because the question was put and I need a response. Was the situation described correctly in that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. It's the same objection. It's hearsay information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, if I asked the question, it was for the witness to confirm that he was kept abreast. Now, according to our ruling, you save your objections to the cross-examination. So we're not going to interrupt the Prosecution's examination-in-chief. I came to your help because I asked the witness whether he was kept abreast, and he has just explained to us that he was kept abreast perfectly. So if you want to go into the matter further, you can do so during your cross-examination time. But allow the Prosecution to conduct its examination-in-chief as they see fit, and then, in the light of what has been said, we will be able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not trying to interrupt their cross-examination. I'm entitled to make a record, and the record is: Now we're asking the witness to vouch for the truthfulness. It's one thing for the gentleman to say, "I received hearsay information." Hearsay information can't come in. I don't have objection to that. But now to vouch for the hearsay information and to say that the hearsay information was true, accurate, and complete, that's where I draw the line, because now we're going into the weight. That's the point that I wish to make. So I have no problems with him saying, "This is what's in the report. This is what I was told." But to vouch for the veracity of what's in there, I believe that's one step too many.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add as I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Stewart. I'll respond to what's just been said. We're talking about hearsay. The witness has just said that he had permanent connection with people from the Spanish Battalion in Mostar, and that that information was in realtime. So where is hearsay information there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hearsay information, Your Honour, is an out-of-court statement offered for the truth of the matter asserted therein. He did not observe it. He's being told. I'm not saying what he's been told is untruthfulness, but I think it goes to the weight. It is hearsay. It's not direct knowledge. He didn't observe it. Had the gentleman observed it, I wouldn't be up here, because then it would be his words and he could be saying, "Yes, this is what I saw, and this is accurately reflected in the report." He's being told, and I think there is a distinction. That's all. I'm not trying to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, I feel some slight guilt here because I certainly signalled to Mr. Karnavas that I supported his objection and encouraged him. So, Your Honour, I would just like to put on record that Mr. Petkovic's counsel do associate themselves 100 per cent. There is difference -- with what Mr. Karnavas says. There is a difference between a witness having told the Court that the reports were reliable generally in his experience, which is entirely legitimate because he was there. Once he's told the Court that the reports were reliable, then the Court can look at the reports. But the witness, as Mr. Karnavas says, is not in a position then to say, "Yes, I personally can verify them." He's told the Court enough. Moreover, Your Honour invited the witness to say whether the Trial Chamber could conclude something. Your Honours, that's a decision for Your Honours; it's not for the witness. The witness tells the Trial Chamber the facts. Whether the Trial Chamber can properly reach the conclusion is ultimately for Your Honours, when Your Honours write your judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This dispute is quite interesting and very, very theoretical. I do not think that it is, in any way, practically, practically, in the effect, at the end of the day, of any use to the Defence. And I think it's an exercise in style. I can understand that counsel engage in this, because that's the way they are trained and that's the rules they are trained in. But it's not universally recognised rules. It's small nuances. And we're really losing time on this. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just a small remark. The document I was referring to is an intsum. I made a difference between intrep and intsum. That was the reason for my question, whether the information was reflected correctly, as came from Madrid, from the higher level. That was the reason for that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, just take a look at your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness wishes to reply. Witness, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report is drafted in the headquarters of the higher unit of the Spanish Battalion, in the chain of command of the Spanish forces, and it's drafted in Madrid. What I can verify is that the information referred to on the 9th of May, 1993, is an accurate reflection of the information provided by my section concerning the events in Mostar on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at your final report, page 34. Final report, page 34, from the words "The day at 5.00 ..." But what I'm interested in, actually, is the passage: "When the fighting started, the SpaBat company, which was in the area, withdrew to safe zones in the vicinity of the Croatian hospital. However, at 12.00, at the request of the HVO, they were compelled to leave the city." Were you really compelled by the HVO to leave the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. As I have already stated, when the bombardment started in the east of Mostar and when there was the exchange of fire, the western-based patrol withdrew to observation points from which they could continue observing events in the city. The zone selected was the parking lot of the Mostar hospital. At 12.00, by radio, the headquarters of the Spanish Battalion learned that the Croatian defence forces patrol had approached the patrol of the Spanish Battalion, and requested or ordered that they leave the area, because if they did not abandon the area, they could get hurt in the exchange of fire. The patrol chief at that time interpreted this order as a threat. He reported that to the headquarters of the Spanish Battalion, and there, the decision was taken for the patrol to leave that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now take a look at page 35 of the same report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. A follow-up to what you've just said, Witness. You said that parts of the Spanish Battalion thought that this was a threat. Now, there are two ways of reading this. Either they wanted to protect them and say, "Don't stay there because otherwise you might be hit by a shell," or they said, "If you stay there, we're going to shoot at you." So what is the exact sense, the exact meaning, of what was said, what the HVO unit said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that particular time, the person that spoke with the Croatian defence forces and asked the Spanish patrol to leave is a Spanish officer, and we understand this as being credible. He interpreted what was said by what has been cited textually, as well as via the attitude shown by the Croatian defence force representatives as a threat, and that's how it was communicated back to us. The head of the Spanish Battalion, given this information, decided to have the troops, the patrol, withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the command of the Spanish Battalion was concerned, the fact of withdrawing, what would that mean? Was it so the observers weren't present? This patrol next to the hospital, what was the reason for their withdrawal? Was it military interest, political interest, or some other interest? So what was the interest in having the international observers withdraw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conclusion that we reached was that there was some interest on the part of the Croatian defence forces in not having any international observers witnessing what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're telling us what happened. Now, to the best of your knowledge, in the town of Mostar -- you were in Medjugorje, but, as you've already said, you had contacts with your comrades there. So, in Mostar, were there any internationals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, yes, there were information media there. I'm not entirely sure, but I understood that the presence of the Spanish Battalion there was uncomfortable for the Croatian defence forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now we'll turn to page 35 of the same report; I mean the passage that starts with the words: "In consequence of the agreement signed by Halilovic and Petkovic ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Halilovic, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you return to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 14th of May, the patrols in Mostar were reunited, and, as the report states, there were observations that there was an increasing frequency of firing upon our patrols. Mainly we were able to detect the origin of this fire on our troops. The fire was coming from the western part of the city, which was the part controlled by the Croatian defence forces. Although I would like to reiterate that I did say "mainly." There were occasions when sometimes the fair came from the armija side, but to a much lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this report you also mentioned, on the previous page, that: "The HVO controls keep the city under total siege." Please, could you explain your conclusion of the total siege. What did you mean by "total siege"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, in all of the roads leading to Mostar, there were check-points staffed by forces from whichever conflicting party dominated that area. This was a practical -- this was a practice that was quite common throughout Bosnia. From 5.00 in the morning, on the 9th of May, these check-points, manned by the Croatian defence forces, prevented any UNPROFOR vehicles from entering the city. Acting in this way, from our point of view, this led to an isolation of the city, and they prevented our access to the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in a -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Poryvaev, I would like to ask a question of the witness, also concerning page 35, the first paragraph. At the very end of that paragraph, there is a sentence which says, and I quote: "To face up to the HVO offensive, the BiH needs to transfer to the city all the units it was using to cover the front with the Serbs so that that territory remains completely unoccupied." Most probably it is due to a translation from Spanish to English, but for me, the very word "unoccupied" would mean "undefended." So most probably the issue was that the territory of -- that territory of Herzegovina which was beyond Mostar, as far as the front line between the BiH, HVO, and the Serb forces, Republika Srpska, that it was not, in a way, unoccupied but undefended. I wonder if the witness would confirm this understanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a military document and sometimes we use military language. When we say "unoccupied," it means it has no military defence capacity. It doesn't mean that it cannot be observed, for example. Quite simply, we noted the fact -- in fact, we received the information that the units of the ABiH, which were staffing these areas, were imprisoned in Mostar next to the boulevard, and they were in opposition to the Croatian defence forces there. Obviously, they left elements there, but they didn't leave any military defence capacity behind them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Witness CB, my next question is about the bridges in Mostar. What happened to bridges during this attack in Mostar as from the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the 9th of May, we observed that there was concentrated fire on certain bridges, which were the bridges used to go from one side of the city to the other, since the city was divided by the river.
