Via reports and conversations with the Croatian defence forces for the development of the operations from a military point of view, we arrived at the conclusion that the Croatian defence forces were attempting to isolate the Muslim part of the city, which was basically on the right riverbank, the east bank of the Neretva River. I'm talking about the Donja Mahala neighbourhood and its surrounding areas, which were controlled by the ABiH. But --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreter corrects: This was on the west side of the river.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw more intense fire on the Tito Bridge and on the bridge known as -- I beg your forgiveness, Your Honour. It was known as the old bridge, but in fact there's a date upon which the bridge could no longer be used for the passage of vehicles. People on foot could pass only. As far as the bridges are concerned, I can't actually give any more information than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to turn to your report, page 34. Final report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's the Bijela bridge. The Bijela bridge is north of Mostar, on the main highway that joins Mostar with Jablanica. So on the 13th of May, this bridge was bombed and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By units of the Croatian defence forces. The intention being of blocking communication via highway between the eastern part of Mostar and the central Jacan part; the Jablanica area, in other words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would like to pass on to another topic that is relevant to the arrest of Muslims. And I would like just not to split in two the periods of time as May, July. Just for the sake of saving time, the whole period of your mission in the area of responsibility, did you observe facts of arrests of Muslims, Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. Apart from the visit to Sovici and Doljani that we mentioned before, in Mostar, from the 9th specifically, we observed civilians being gathered in the football field and later on taken by bus to the area known as Heliodrom. I personally did not go to the Heliodrom, but I informed that staff from my section did visit the Heliodrom - and there are reports regarding this - and so did other international organisations, other members from UNPROFOR, such as UN military units and Red Cross, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge about the arrests of Muslims further, I mean after May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Mostar, in the Mostar area, from the 9th of May, an operation began by the security forces of the Croatian defence forces. This operation ended up in detention of all the Muslims who were living in the eastern part of Mostar. Aside from that, I don't really know the exact date, but as a result of the counter-attack launched by the armija BiH, an operation which led to occupying the northern headquarters and the southern part of Mostar, the south-east of Mostar more specifically, a series of events took place and Muslims were, once again, detained en masse from villages between Capljina and Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to turn to Exhibit 3271, page 5. 3271. 3271.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a report drafted by the UNPROFOR headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who provided information to UNPROFOR headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the information regarding the Spanish Battalion sector results from the report drafted by my section on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, my next question, that's about the Heliodrom. So did you have free access to Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the entire time of the operation, and mainly from the 9th of May onward, freedom of movement, our freedom of movement, was very restricted. We could only go to places where we were allowed to go. We couldn't force entry anywhere. One of the areas or places which were beyond our reach was or were the installations of the Heliodrom. It was only when it was possible to reach agreement at a relatively high level - what I'm talking about is either intervention from the Chief of Staff of the Croatian defence forces or General Lasic in charge of the area - only if that was agreed we could go jointly with the international organisations, such as the Red Cross, if I'm not mistaken. However, we couldn't just go whenever we wanted and so on. It always depended on a pre-agreement, and we were always accompanied by members of the Croatian defence forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, did you get your first information about the prisoners at Heliodrom from other organisations? Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I seem to remember that the first information we received on what was inside the Heliodrom came from the United Nations Military Observers. And I would say that -- I refer to within the Heliodrom, because what our patrols were able to observe was that the personnel gathered in the football field would be transported by bus, with a military escort, towards the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to look at Exhibit 2414. That's SpaBat intrep 173, dated the 15th of May. English, page 5; Spanish, page 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a report prepared by my section which is based on the report prepared by the military observers of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this intrep describes what was happening inside the Heliodrom facilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. This is the information that was given to us by the UN military observers after they visited these installations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next exhibit, 2446. English, page 5; Spanish, page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the information resulting from that visit, which I personally was not involved in but some representative of my section did take part. I can't remember exactly who it was at this stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge about some other detention facilities on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina run by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Croatian defence forces side, we got information from other detention centres, such as Gabela, and I, myself, visited Dretelj. When I went to Dretelj, it was a military barracks outside Capljina, and I went to interview the military staff of the unit which was assigned to those installations. So going to the offices of the commander-in-chief of this military unit, I observed staff carrying out cleaning activities, and that person was escorted by armed military staff. So when I asked who this staff was, they quite naturally told us that they were war prisoners interned in this camp, and they were used to carry out maintenance tasks in these installations. We were not allowed, although we asked for that, to visit the installations where these people were lodged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you have an opportunity of visiting the west part of Mostar, just in the period from May through, let's say, September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As we said, from the end of April onwards, quite a number of meetings took place, and agreements come to with the intention of putting them into effect. On several occasions I was able to go to Mostar, the eastern part as well as the western part, to interview those in charge of the Croatian defence forces as well as the armija BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just claimed here in the courtroom that East Mostar was isolated at some point. When did you get a first chance of visiting East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd like to repeat that we're talking of military reports. So when it is said that one area is isolated, it means militarily isolated. We were able to have access to eastern Mostar with the authorisation of the Croatian defence forces. So either we crossed the so-called Tito Bridge, or one could enter eastern Mostar from the highway coming from the south, southern part of the city, from where the airport is. In either case, it was necessary to have the authorisation of the Croatian defence forces. Otherwise, it was impossible, because check-points just stopped anybody from coming in. In spite of having had the authorisation from the Croatian defence forces, there were occasions where the staff in charge of one or another check-point would block our way, would not let us have access, even if we showed them the authorisation obtained, signed personally by General Petkovic. But there were situations where the staff in charge of the check-points took no notice of these authorisations. I would like to repeat that, in spite of all that, I visited both eastern and western Mostar on several occasions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your observations about the humanitarian situation in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In eastern Mostar, the situation reached a critical level. There was no food, but not to an extreme level. We were much more concerned by the fact that there was no drinking water, because the population was going straight to the Neretva River to get water, with the resulting complications that might arise from that. The health of the population, the condition in which all the sanitary installations were in eastern Mostar, that was really very serious. One hospital was over-full and had to resort to very few medicines answer material necessary for doctors to carry out their work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did the military convoys have free access to East Mostar? I'm sorry, humanitarian convoys, not military convoys. Humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not have free access. Every time a humanitarian convoy wanted to go to eastern Mostar, that had to be negotiated beforehand with representatives of the Croatian defence forces and reach some sort of agreement with them. And these negotiations to gain access could take days, weeks even. And when an agreement was reached, the Croatian defence forces demanded distribution amongst Croatian refugees in Mostar and Ljubuski, for example. They came from Central Bosnia mainly. And even so, there were occasions, after having obtained an agreement and all the authorisations required, we reached one check-point, so what happened then was that the humanitarian convoy and the escorting Spanish Battalion forces were forced to turn back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When that agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every humanitarian aid convoy was subject to a special agreement for its entry into Mostar. So every time that we were informed of a humanitarian convoy ready to enter Mostar, we had to contact the Croatian defence forces and enter into negotiation with them. These negotiations sometimes could take days. Usually, there were present in these negotiations some ACNUR representative there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: It seems to me we can take a break now, before I pass to the second -- to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will then take a break. Registrar, will you please tell me how much time the Prosecutor has used up so far, but I believe he has another hour left available to him. You have already used 127 minutes -- 125 minutes. Anyway, we are now going for a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in several reports you refer to the facts of sniping the international vehicles and some violent actions with respect to soldiers and members of several humanitarian organisations. What were your knowledge -- what was your knowledge about those facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly, as of the second entry of the patrols in Mostar, and here I'm talking about the 14th of May, 1993, it could be observed that our patrols were fired upon with increasing frequency. The reports of the patrols reflect these facts and, furthermore, this can be observed in the damage incurred by our vehicles. Similarly, we received reports from other members of the international community, for example, military observers of the UN, of these facts to such an extent that these observers actually had to leave the city of Mostar because they did not have the means of protection for their staff necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to turn to Exhibit 2423. That's SpaBat intrep 175, 17th of May, 1993. English, page -- pages 5-6; Spanish, page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand that you're referring to the final paragraph in which there is an item of information concerning convoy drivers of trucks which were part of the humanitarian aid convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was common practice to subject these humanitarian aid convoys to searches on many occasions, and this was carried out by those staffing the check-points. Very often, these staff demanded either a payment in cash or a certain proportion of the cargo in order to let the vehicle through. This happened despite the fact that the convoys did have the corresponding authority for free passage. Furthermore, these drivers, if they tried to defend the cargo that they were transporting, there were occasions where they were physically -- they were victims of physical aggression. And all of these reports did come back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to turn to Exhibit 2844. English, pages 2-3; Spanish, also pages 2-3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's about UNMO vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I do personally recall receiving military observers in this vehicle, and verified the damage that the vehicle had received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is a conclusion in paragraph two: "The gunfire came from the west zone and actually hit one of the vehicles." Is that correct? And who investigated this fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the Spanish Battalion, given the impact on the vehicles and the position of the vehicle at the time when it received this damage, the members of the Spanish Battalion, with technical knowledge in terms of being able to identify the source of fire, did actually arrive at the conclusion that they came from positions occupied by Croatian defence forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to turn to your final report, page 36. Just from the words, "In the city, incident follows incident ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A humanitarian aid convoy which had had its cargo destroyed in both parts, after it had unloaded its cargo in the west part, the drivers were held. The Spanish Battalion intervened, and they communicated with our interlocutors in the Croatian defence forces and managed to get our drivers released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, what were your personal observations of the shelling of East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I repeat that, from a military point of view, and depending on how the situation was developing, it seemed clear to us that the intention of the operations of the Croatian defence forces had as its objective that the civilian population leave East Mostar. The logic behind this was confirmed to us by members of the Croatian defence forces themselves, who argued that once the civilian population left East Mostar, the forces of the armija would no longer have a reason to be there and the Croatian defence forces would have had a successful operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, sir, could you be a bit more precise -- [Spanish on English channel]. Could you tell us who it was and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This particular phrase, that once the civilian population had left East Mostar, the defenders of the ABiH would no longer have any reason to be there, was by Slobodan Bozic. Sometimes he was called the Minister of Defence within the Croatian defence forces; at other times he was introduced as an official liaison person. He was our point of contact, our main point of contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you heard him, with your own ears, say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were used by the warring factions in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area of Mostar, when it came to the Croatian defence forces, they used all kinds of armament that they had in their possession at that time, from artillery of a large-size calibre to lighter weapons. On the armija BiH side, I recall that we did find some mortars of 125 calibre. There weren't many of them. And those were the largest sized weapons we found in that area. On the Croatian defence forces side, there was a wide range of armament, from lots of different kinds and from lots of different places. Personally, I remember artillery of 155-millimetre calibre and anti-aircraft cannons, which were used for firing from the land. And these were located around the Hum suburbs. And there was more than one tank. I remember one tank, the T-35 model, which was found on the top of Mount Hum. The civilians and combatants in East Mostar were particularly fearful of this tank. Because of the way it was perched at this vantage point, it could have find very accurately on to any part of the east part of the Mostar city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, a question that the Judges are highly interested in: Was there any technical possibility for the Serbs -- that the Serbs could have shot at Mostar, targeted Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in our reports, they did reflect the fact that at times we observed impacts whose origin was actually difficult to identify, but it seemed to be that these impacts were caused by firing from the Serbian lines. And this coincided with periods of relative calm in the city, which led us to believe that, obviously, after these impacts, activity in the city increased and there was a greater exchange of fire between both parties. This led us to believe that the Serbs, who had a dominant position over the city of Mostar, were following and monitoring activities in the city, and when activity increased, they tried to stir up these conflicts even more by firing as much at one side as the other. So they would fire just as much into the east side as the west side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a hypotheses that the headquarters of the Spanish Battalion put forward, or do you say that on the basis of indisputable elements, that this could have been the case? Because you've just told us that the Serbs saw that between the Muslims and the Croats there was less tension; then they would ignite tensions by firing a few shots, by well-targeted action. Is that what you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only way to determine a force is to carry out a detailed analysis of the impact, and what we were living through at that particular time made it impossible for us to conduct this kind of detailed analysis. However, the data that we did have concerning these specific impacts led us to believe that they had not come from the Croatian defence forces' positions, nor from the armija. So the only logical conclusion was that one, that they came from afar. For us, it was clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, just my question: What about the correlations of impacts from the Croat side and the Muslim side? Because they were just shooting at each other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, the volume of firing from the western part, the Croatian defence forces part, towards the east of the city was much greater than the returning fire from the armija's positions. This is perfectly -- easily explainable because the number of heavy weapons in the Croatian defence forces' territory was considerably greater than the weapons held by armija.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to turn to Exhibit 2414. English version, page 4; Spanish, 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mostar shelling, this part of the report. They say about the frequency, "discharged every two minutes." Was it actually the case in May, 1993, from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The information which was drawn from direct observation was that artillery and mortar fire had been observed at a rate of once every two minutes, between the hours stipulated or reflected in the report. Moreover, there is a small pause and then fire resumes, but at this stage, instead of being artillery and mortar fire, it was rocket-launchers. I can't remember the exact technical characteristics of these rocket-launchers, but I remember that they were rocket-launchers that were mobile and they had once been the property of the former People's Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Next exhibit, 2423. That's about the shelling of the 17th of May. English, page 5; Spanish, page 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mention here "SpaBat calculation." Who was or who were those persons who were making those calculations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our very own patrols managed to have a record of the explosions that occurred in the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the shelling continue further? I mean, during the summertime, in the autumn 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military operations in Mostar continued throughout our whole stay in the area, the whole stay of my battalion. The intensity varied, naturally. It wasn't always as intense as day in question, the 17th of May, but the conflict and the exchange of fire and shelling continued throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please now take a look at Exhibit 8 -- sorry, 4813. Intrep 286, 5th of September, 1993. I mean the passage that starts with the words "Seventy-five explosions ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that correlation can be such as indicated in this report: Four, five, in the Croat area and the rest in the Muslim area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I repeat: This is a direct observation from the Spanish Battalion personnel. Among other things in the reports, they had to provide a reflection of these explosions that they observed, and they had to differentiate between the different areas from whence these explosions came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you receive information, reports, about any casualties as a result of those shellings in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I received information, and I also observed the results of these explosions in my visits to East Mostar. I recall visiting on more than one occasion the East Mostar hospital and witnessing the bodies and cadavers deposited there. And I saw many burials in the cemeteries, these ad hoc cemeteries which were set up in East Mostar, notably in public parks. The public parks were used for burials for those who had passed away in the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like to take a look at Exhibit 409 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask for a question in between?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, have you ever noted, do you know anything about, a mortar of the ABiH being in position near the hospital in East Mostar? Does that mean something to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we observed a position. We saw some mortars in East Mostar. Near the hospital? Well, yes, relatively near the hospital. We, at that time, had the impression that - again, I repeat, from a military point of view - we thought these mortars were positioned where they could be located. Their presence at the hospital, well, they weren't right behind the hospital or right next to it. They were relatively close to the hospital. But, really, in the East Mostar area, there was very little space available to -- very little space for positioning a weapon of that size.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit 4951. English, page 5; Spanish, page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which paragraph were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The Muslim quarter was shelled during the morning."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, this information was provided by the patrol. As being -- reflected here, the patrol suffered -- was very close to shelling, and you could see how the casualties were transferred to the hospital in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Next exhibit, 4995. English, page 5; Spanish, page 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Today, 60 artillery ..." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it, the final paragraph talking about the shelling of Mostar. Here, again, information provided by the patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They talk about three people dead and two wounded. Were there any casualties among your SpaBat soldiers in East Mostar as a result of shelling or sniping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the area of Mostar, we suffered two dead and several wounded - I can't remember the exact number of wounded now - in various activities. I remember the two dead; they were two officers. One was the result of shelling and the other was the result of a sniper attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the damage caused by the shelling in the area controlled by the Muslim part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The east part of Mostar mainly was left like any war-torn zone. It was destroyed. Many, many buildings were structurally damaged. The area of the boulevard, which was the confrontation line throughout the period of conflict, was completely destroyed. There was not one single building left in a usable state. And on the other side of the river, the Donja Mahala neighbourhood, the area covered by the armija on the western bank was completely destroyed, and the area on the east, almost entirely destroyed. Very few buildings were left untouched in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to turn to your final report, page 84.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have very few questions left. I'm very disciplined and I will finalise my examination-in-chief today/this evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 84?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. "Use of tanks." Okay. If I'm wrong, just -- no reference to the document, just your knowledge of the use of tanks by -- during that war. Okay. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's page 87 in the Spanish version of the final report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We observed the use of tanks mainly by the Croatian defence forces, which is logical, actually, because in our area of responsibilities, the landscape, from a military point of view, made it very difficult for tanks to be used in the area controlled by the armija. From a military point of view, I repeat: Tanks were used more as a mobile item of artillery than a combat vehicle itself. And to talk about the well-known Mount Hum tank, we found other tanks as well, very modern tanks, T-55, for example, in the immediate surroundings, in the immediate suburbs, of Mostar, and when you leave Mostar, heading towards Ljubuski, there were tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this paragraph, it is stated clearly that the HVO used four to six tanks, T-55, that caused great damage in Muslim settlements, and also that some BH army members were wounded as a result of this action. You say these tanks were used in Jablanica and Doljani as well. This summary written about the tanks, is it based on what members of the Spanish Battalion saw with their own eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the paragraph on page 87, which begins with the letter L, talking about tanks, is a summary of what was observed and reflected in the daily reports drafted by the Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CB, what is your personal knowledge about the HV involvement in the armed conflict between HVO and ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm going to try and divide the knowledge I have of this subject into the area of Mostar and the area of Jablanica. In the Mostar area, mainly stemming from the counter-attack launched by armija in which the northern barracks, Tihomir Misic, and the confrontation line was shifted towards Bijelo Polje and Potoci, we started to observe the presence of staff, of personnel, and materiel which showed emblems of the army of the Republic of Croatia. In the area of Ploce, where we had a liaison officer with the UNHCR, from there, the humanitarian aid convoys set out. And around the depots of the UNHCR, there was a military base of the army of the Republic of Croatia, and we saw vehicles and personnel heading north towards Mostar. Later, in the very city itself of Mostar, we observed -- again, I saw just as much staff and vehicles which were clearly identified as belonging to army of the Republic of Croatia. This was in the area of Mostar. In the story of Jablanica, the personnel with whom we had relations of the armija BiH informed us that in the Croatian bags, in the pockets, in the enclaves of that area, there were -- that they had observed Croatian army personnel. Personally, I received two ID cards which, according to the members of the armija, these were ID cards from soldiers that were killed in the area, and these ID cards, I repeat, were of the army of the Republic of Croatia. Moreover, on more than one occasion I was shown a body which, according to the sources in the armija, had been recovered in the north of Jablanica, and they were wearing the uniform with the distinctive insignia of the Croatian army. And I personally saw the coat of arms on that uniform, on that body, and it was from the army of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You seem to make a distinction between Jablanica and Mostar. I'd like to come to Mostar. Did you personally, with your own eyes, see vehicles or troops belonging to the Republic of Croatia? You said they had insignia, patches, but did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us more precisely the day, the hour, the place - if you remember, of course - the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recall with the most precision what I was talking about close to Jablanica, because, I repeat, at that time I was sent there by my section and I received -- I received the ID cards in my hand, and the patch. I saw the body myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about Jablanica, whereas I am referring to Mostar, I'm focusing on Mostar. Did you see in Mostar, after the BH offensive, the arrival of troops, apparently coming from the Republic of Croatia, with equipment and weapons? Did you see that with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw in the western part of Mostar the odd vehicle in which you could clearly see the number plate of the army of the Republic of Croatia, "HV," perfectly distinguishable from the Croatian defence force plates, which were HVO. And inside I saw that the personnel were wearing the coat of arms -- the patch with the coat of arms of the army of Republic of Croatia. More concrete detail, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I would not be able to give you right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question. Was it a military vehicle you just told Their Honours about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I personally remember seeing a light vehicle, a jeep kind, and two or three lorries. I can't remember precisely. Now, the rear part of the lorries was covered up, and I ignored whether they were transporting people or materiel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to Jablanica. I would like you to take a look at Exhibit 3705. That's English, page 8-10; Spanish, 2-4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd like to state vis-a-vis this report, which was written the 25th of July -- the 25th of July, I was in Jablanica's detachment. That is why the information on the vehicles going from Dracevo to Medjugorje is not directly done by myself. It was provided by some of our patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Next exhibit, 3724. English, page 4; Spanish, page 3-4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, you can see two types of information about the same matter. The first one, you can see it in page number 3. These are the routes between Grude-Ljubuski-Metkovici-Dracevo. And I've got to say exactly the same thing: These are the reports of the 25th of July. I was in Jablanica. All the information vis-a-vis this area Jablanica/Konjic, I did myself, I provided that information myself. And here is where you can see the information vis-a-vis the military ID. And on page number 6, Spanish version, you can see the drawing I did myself of the armband that I observed in the corpse or in the body that was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last group of questions, Witness, you have already explained to the Trial Chamber that at some point, at some point, there were some facts of shelling of BSA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you want to say, Mr. Praljak? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] We have discussed this King Tomislav affair many times. A couple of exhibits have been introduced. Mr. Alija Izetbegovic first proclaimed it a regiment of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was composed of Croats and Muslims who, in April in 1994, prepared themselves in Basko Polje, and Zuka was one of them. He had --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't know if this is an objection or a statement. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I just wanted to ask this. It's objection. We just wanted to -- I think we just need to clarify this immediately, because we keep coming back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We don't. We don't. I have stated before, and Mr. Karnavas agreed, that when there are objections to what a witness said, that can be dealt with later on but it's not a reason to interrupt immediately. This is just disrupting, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will continue. Yes. You just explained to the Trial Chamber that there were some facts of shelling on Mostar on the part of BSA. Do you know anything about the involvement of BSA in the armed conflict on the whole -- on the territory of Mostar city or the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the area of your responsibility and area of influence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to pinpoint that during April up to October of 1993, the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina was very complicated. The circumstances in Mostar were totally different to what was happening in Jablanica and had nothing to do with Maglaj or Bihac, and so on. So both the reports from the headquarter of UNPROFOR, they were talking about collaborations in the reports between some of the parts of the Croatian council or the ABiH with the BSA. In the area of responsibility of the Spanish Battalion, we observed in Jablanica, mainly in Ljubina, the area which was at the western area of Konjic, the city of Konjic, where we observed that there was collaboration between those who were defending this area, which belonged to the Croatian forces, and the BSA. This collaboration mainly was supported with artillery, artillery support. The ABiH launched several offences against this area, against this pocket, and they were rejected by the artillery barriers, fire barriers, from the positions of the Serb -- the Serbian and Bosnian army. And that area, that, so to speak, pocket, was totally isolated. But I remember when visiting that part, I remember seeing that the munition was not lacking, and I remember even seeing strange movements, strange movements amongst the staff, which seemed to belong to the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to take a look at Exhibit 2979. This is a Kiseljak headquarters report, dated the 27th of June, 1993. Page, actually, 10, and page 9 -- page 9 in e-court, yes. Page 6 in e-court. Yes, yes. Page 6 on e-court. Page 7. Yes, page 7 and paragraph 2; and page 10, hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder if counsel could just give a paragraph number. Many of these documents are paragraphed, and there are rather a lot of page numbers given in that brief introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: It's paragraph 5 and paragraph 2. Yes, Your Honour, just one second. Everything is all right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the situation you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, where are we? Paragraph 5 and paragraph 2, and page 6 and page 7 and page 9. All through this examination, counsel has either not given paragraph numbers or given the wrong ones. But really now I'm simply lost. Please, where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: First of all, it's the first time that I make such kind of error. No need to invent things here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us the page number. We have it on the screen. It's 16 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Page 6 of 8. The ERN, the last digits, 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: On the screen, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's page 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The comment on the situation and the operations in the area at Jablanica-Konjic is a reflection, a truthful reflection, of the comments of my section in the daily reports -- in the daily reports of the previous day of the issuing of this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was final question. I'm very thankful to the witness for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. As for admission of evidence, you will do it as envisaged by the decision, which means you'll make a schedule and then we will mark the numbers which will help us all gain time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I will have that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Defence, you have three hours, as envisaged, tomorrow. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I have a request, Your Honours. As we have only one witness, obviously, and he's a professional military man, who very swiftly went through heaps of documents, including a huge number of statements, "I have seen, I haven't seen, we found out," et cetera, it is not possible to follow at that speed, and I would be very grateful if you could grant me and General Petkovic some more time so as to be able to arrive at precise facts that could establish the truth in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Picking up where General Praljak left off, Your Honour, it would appear that much of the testimony that we heard today has already been heard from previous witnesses, and I point this out because I know we're trying to save time and trying to be efficient. Well, I have a criticism of the Prosecution. I think that a lot of this information is cumulative and it's repetitive. But when they introduce all these documents, it does force the Defence, then, to spend a lot of valuable time in court going over that. So I join General Praljak's request, but I would also request from the Trial Chamber to perhaps instruct the Prosecutor to go back and to make sure that when they bring a witness, such as this gentleman, who has come from very far away - and, incidentally, he was a marvelous witness, marvelous both in the way he answered the questions, very precise, very careful, didn't speculate; so I commend you, sir, and we're grateful that you're here - but nonetheless, I think we could have saved the UN some money and saved ourselves a little bit of time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard both parties. We will discuss it again among Judges tomorrow, and we will answer Mr. Praljak's request. For the moment, we have decided to give everybody, together, three hours to be divided as you see fit. You can give Mr. Praljak two hours, if you wish, or you can give him the entire cross-examination time. Anyway, tomorrow we will impart to you our decision regarding his request that some other Defence counsel have seconded. It is time to call it a day. We will reconvene tomorrow at 2.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
